title: Scripture and Oral Tradition
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a text sacred to a community and how some traditions passed scripture down by memory for centuries.
summary: A scripture is a text a community reveres as carrying sacred power or revelation, gathered into a canon. Most began as oral tradition, like the Vedas and the Buddhist Pali canon.

cards.headline: Some of the world's oldest scriptures spent centuries with no pages at all.
cards.body: Most sacred texts started out spoken, carried in memory from teacher to student. What makes a text sacred, and how do you keep one word-perfect without writing it down?

cards.headline: What makes a text sacred
cards.body: Scriptures are texts a community reveres because they are believed to carry spiritual power, or to be the way a divine being or sacred reality is revealed. Over time the most sacred ones are gathered into a canon: a fixed collection held fully authoritative, settled by general agreement or by official religious bodies. So a text doesn't become scripture by being old or beautiful. It becomes scripture because a community receives it that way.

cards.headline: Memory before ink
cards.body: Most scriptures began as oral traditions, memorized and passed down, generation after generation, until someone wrote them down. The Vedas, which Hindus regard as shruti, "what is heard", were composed from about 1500 BCE, most scholars estimate, and preserved by voice. Reciters are taught from childhood techniques based on tonal accents and exact pronunciation, so the sound of every word stays unaltered. Think of it as a backup system made of people.

cards.headline: Written down, still spoken
cards.body: Buddhist teachings were memorized and recited by monks for generations; the Pali canon was first written down in Sri Lanka, probably in the 1st century BCE. Writing didn't end the spoken life of scripture, though. The Quran's name means "recitation", and verses from it are recited in the five daily prayers.

cards.headline: Scripture and Oral Tradition: the takeaways
learned: Scripture is a text a community reveres as sacred
Canons are fixed by agreement or by religious authorities
Many scriptures lived for centuries in memory and voice

questions.prompt: How were most sacred scriptures first passed down?

options.label: By memory, from generation to generation
Carved on stone tablets for public display
Printed in books for every household
Kept secret by a single family line
options.rationale: They were taught and recited widely.

questions.explanation: Most scriptures were originally oral, memorized and passed down until they were written.

questions.prompt: What turns a collection of sacred texts into a canon?

options.label: Being the oldest writings in a language
A government printing office approving the text
options.rationale: It's the community or its religious bodies.

options.label: A community or its religious bodies fixing which works count

questions.explanation: Canons are fixed by general agreement or by official religious bodies.

questions.prompt: What do the Vedas and the Buddhist Pali canon share?

options.label: Both were first written in Arabic
Both were kept by memory and recitation
Both were composed in Sri Lanka
options.rationale: Only the Pali canon was written down there.

options.label: Both were banned from being spoken aloud
options.rationale: Both were meant to be recited.

questions.explanation: The Vedas were preserved orally, and the Pali canon was memorized for generations before it was written down in Sri Lanka.
